According to recent reports, every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

One evening in November, Celia Rowlson-Hall slipped into a conference room for a rare break. The choreographer has spent the past four weeks rehearsing a fresh Off-Broadway revival of Spring Awakening, directed by Tony winner Danya Taymor, and it’s the second day of tech week. She had been holed up in Studio Seaview’s adjacent theater, fine-tuning “The Bitch of Living,” an angsty number about wet dreams, busty piano teachers, and Nietzsche. Previews were set to begin in a little over a week, and Rowlson-Hall eagerly tucked into a takeout grain bowl, fueling up for her evening ahead.

Set in 19th-century Germany, Spring Awakening is about the turmoil of developing sexuality in teenagers in a society attempting to keep them in ignorance. In 2006, the playwright Steven Sater and the musician Duncan Sheik adapted it into a musical that won eight Tony Awards, including for choreographer Bill T. Jones, who translated rebellion and repression into a gestural vocabulary. That original production also launched a generation of musical theater stars, including Jonathan Groff, Lea Michele, and John Gallagher Jr. In this spirit, the production held an open audition that attracted 2,532 performers (two actors were cast from this process). Rowlson-Hall kept her eye out for those actors with a sense of grounded earthiness and truthful storytelling. “I’m always going to be looking out for authenticity and personality inside of movement,” she says. “I don't care about the pointed foot or the high leg; it's never interested me, even as a dancer. I've never understood dance for dance’s sake.”.

In a recent development, spring Awakening will mark Rowlson-Hall’s theatrical debut after nearly two decades of directing and choreographing for screen. Among her work are the scenes of ecstatic prayer in The Testament of Ann Lee and Aftersun’s devastating rave sequence (she also played the adult version of the lead character). Humorously, she recently appeared in The Drama as a dance teacher intent on perfection, a mentality that couldn’t be farther from Rowlson-Hall’s own intuitive and empathetic style.

With major blue eyes and a choppy mop of dark hair, Rowlson-Hall, 42, is expressive even when sequestered behind a conference room desk. She frequently puts her fork down to gesture, including when recalling a friend’s suggestion “that all artists have one or two rocks that they will turn over their entire lives.” Rolling a pair of invisible stones around in her palms, she names religion and femininity as her thematic preoccupations. “The impact of religion in the body, specifically the female body, and what femininity looks like as taught to me by my parents versus from society and my own experiences.” She laughs, adding, “As my other friend remarked, ‘Celia loves a repression era.’”.

According to recent reports, like the characters in Spring Awakening, Rowlson-Hall grew up in a small, religious community. In her case, it was Urbanna, Virginia, population 492 as of 2020, in a Christian Scientist household. She started dancing at 5 and knew from a young age that she wanted to use movement to tell stories of her own. After studying at the North Carolina School of the Arts, Rowlson-Hall moved to Upcoming York in 2006, the same year Spring Awakening premiered. “I remember hearing about the show, but also being too poor to go,” she notes.

Two years later, she was planning to start her own dance company when she was asked to choreograph a music video for MGMT. She immediately felt at home on a film set, and also appreciated that the medium offered a more enduring result than a concert dancen ephemeral live performance. “The forever part,” she claims. “I needed it then in my life.” She continued working on music videos, commercials, and television, absorbing lessons on filmmaking along the way. After a series of movement-based feminist shorts, Rowlson-Hall used Kickstarter to finance her first feature, Ma (2015), in which she stars in the dialogue-free dance film as a modern-day Virgin Mary on a pilgrimage to Las Vegas.

Rowlson-Hall met her now-wife, director and showrunner Mia Lidofsky, while choreographing Girls’ acclaimed “Beach House” episode in 2013. Rowlson-Hall was in a heterosexual marriage at the time, and she describes coming out at 30 as “this incredible aha moment.” But then, “Shame came in and clamped me down. I stopped moving.” It was a confusing contrast: while experiencing a profound sense of freedom and selfhood, she became disconnected from her body for the first time. Rowlson-Hall is anxious to elaborate. “The impact of me coming out was very difficult on my family, they initially had a hard time accepting it,” she indicates. “Then my mom got very ill, and I put my life and body on pause because I was so scared for her.” From there followed a decade of extreme highs (falling in love, marriage, motherhood) and lows (divorce, several deaths including both parents). “There were a lot of roadblocks for me to be able to find physicality and movement again because I kept getting knocked down,” she says.

Sources indicate that she credits Ann Lee with allowing her to feel that connection again. The writer and director, Mona Fastvold, is a close friend; the two met back in the day on Gossip Girl. Rowlson-Hall was eager to inhabit the 18th century visionary, an illiterate blacksmith's daughter who became the founder and leader of the Shakers. “As a kid, I used to love to pray, it was my favorite thing,” she notes. “I really wanted to ask myself ‘what if I got to decide what prayer looks like?’” She could also relate to the Shakers’ use of dance as transcendence. “From when I was young, I always felt like I was needing to exorcise things out of my body that weren't mine,” Rowlson-Hall says. “So much of what I do is trying to clear out to actually understand who I am.” The viscera is not strictly a metaphor. “When I feel like I'm going to vomit, I know that I've tapped into the right thing,” she says. “I choreograph from there, and then I can't touch it again.” She makes a gagging sound. “And then it's out of my body.”.

Sources indicate that rowlson-Hall returned to the stage last year with Sissy, a semi-autobiographical dance-theater piece reimagining the myth of Sisyphus as the struggles of a female artist tasked with caring for a young child and an ill father. “There's something about theater and motherhood that feel very aligned,” she indicates with a laugh. “It's all alive and happening in front of you, and you've got to love it and let it go. It journeys on without you, you actually have no control.” That said, she’s working on her next film, which she describes as “a time traveling love story of Eve and Lilith exiting the Garden of Eden” and spending lifetimes together and apart. “There they are again,” Rowlson-Hall says. “Those old stones.”.

The Best Japanese Restaurants in London, From Omakase Counters to Neighborhood Gems

📅 29 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that finding good Japanese food in London hasn’t always been the easiest task, given the city’s abundance of mediocre sushi takeaway spots and gaudy central London restaurants serving sub-par fish dressed up with too many bells and whistles.
  • But in truth, you don’t need to break the bank to eat Japanese food well in London: just take the well-priced lunch set menu at Kiku Mayfair, or the reliably fresh sushi at any Eat Tokyo outpost, or the excellent quality-to-price ratio at Bond Street institution Chisou.
  • From exclusive six-seat counters to beloved West End izakayas, here is our definitive guide to the Japanese restaurants in London that are truly worth the hype.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that finding good Japanese food in London hasn’t always been the easiest task, given the city’s abundance of mediocre sushi takeaway spots and gaudy central London restaurants serving sub-par fish dressed up with too many bells and whistles. (No piece of sushi has ever needed gold leaf so liberally applied.) Historically, to eat well, you’ve had to splurge: it isn’t cheap, after all, to source top-quality fish in the British capital, and it’s still worth saving your pennies for a blowout meal at one of the city’s top omakase counters, such as Sushi Kanesaka or Sushi Tetsu.

But in truth, you don’t need to break the bank to eat Japanese food well in London: just take the well-priced lunch set menu at Kiku Mayfair, or the reliably fresh sushi at any Eat Tokyo outpost, or the excellent quality-to-price ratio at Bond Street institution Chisou. (Its former location next to the old Condé Nast offices on Hanover Square led it to be nicknamed the “Vogue canteen.”) And that’s without mentioning beloved neighborhood spots like Uchi Hackney or Jin Kichi in Hampstead.

From exclusive six-seat counters to beloved West End izakayas, here is our definitive guide to the Japanese restaurants in London that are truly worth the hype.

Located within the ritzy 45 Park Lane hotel, this Michelin-starred, omakase-only destination with 13 seats is as atmospheric a sushi experience as you’ll find anywhere in London. Step through the discreet noren curtain that marks the entrance, and you’ll feel as if you entered a portal straight to Kyoto, with the gently lit interiors—all hinoki wood, lime plaster walls, and intricate kumiko lattice work—serving as a delicate backdrop for the equally delicate flight of dishes that follows. Helmed by legendary chef Shinji Kanesaka, the 13-seat restaurant offers a masterclass in traditional Edomae-style omakase using an impressive array of locally sourced ingredients: a silky pot of chawanmushi topped with the briny sweetness of fresh Cornish crab; marbled, melt-in-your-mouth fatty tuna nigiri with perfectly seasoned rice sourced from Japan’s Yamagata Prefecture; a Scottish lobster presented on a board then whizzed up into shatteringly crisp morsels of tempura. With a price tag of £420 per person, it isn’t for the faint of heart—but for those seeking true perfection, it’s London’s ultimate bucket-list sushi destination. —Liam Hess.

Recent findings suggest that A true Mayfair stalwart, Kiku has been serving the neighborhood since 1978, making it one of the oldest Japanese restaurants in the city—and unlike some of its flashier neighboring sushi restaurants, Kiku’s vibe is one of calm, quiet elegance. It’s the place to go for a consistently excellent, no-frills sushi experience where the quality of the fish speaks for itself, whether it’s the salmon and tuna in a classic sashimi set, or rare delicacies like Hokkaido sea urchin and sweet prawn served on perfectly seasoned rice. The tempura here is world-class, with a light, lace-like batter, and the £40 lunchtime set menu—which consists of yakitori, tempura, sushi, miso soup, and a dessert—is one of the best deals in central London. The ultimate seal of approval? It’s a favorite spot among the staff at the nearby Japanese Embassy on Piccadilly. —L.H.

This low-key but stylish joint, which opened in 2024 in a bijou shopfront on Brewer Street, is the brainchild of chef Takamasa Mogi—also the founder of popular Mayfair spot Cubé—and serves up astonishingly good sushi to the 10 seats that surround its subdued but stylish hinoki wood counter. (Soho regulars will remember the building’s former life as a manga store and karaoke bar—it turns out there’s still a karaoke room downstairs if your omakase dinner ends up getting a little raucous.) I was especially impressed by the creative but not overdone nigiri, including smoky slivers of seared Korean turbot and Spanish tuna with Oscietra caviar, served atop pillowy beds of red vinegar-seasoned rice. Given the quality, it’s excellent value too: the lunchtime menu offers salad, seven pieces of omakase nigiri, and dessert for £51.80, while the dinner menu of two appetizers, nine pieces of omakase nigiri, a temaki roll, and dessert comes to £89. (They also do a well-priced pre-theater menu if you’re planning to catch a West End show.) —L.H.

Under former Noma sommelier Yuki Kaneko’s ownership, Yuki Bar has transcended East London’s small plates and orange wine scene. Within the low-lit, 20-cover spot soundtracked by disco J-pop, dishes riff on French and Nordic classics with Japanese inflections, like a sesame-studded take on oeufs mayonnaise, embracing home-style cooking and a choose-your-own-adventure menu of “snacks, littles, and larges.” A few portions of house-made potato crisps with sansho pepper and grilled onigiri kick the evening off, while rotating mains have included an aromatic chicken hot pot and blushing strips of beef tataki silken with soy sauce and mustard. Go with a group, be greedy, and get a few bottles recommended by Kaneko. —Anna Cafolla.

Sources indicate that mayfair isn’t exactly short on high-end sushi counters, so it takes serious pedigree to make a splashy entrance here. One of the few people capable of that is Shogo Amamoto, the Fukuoka-born chef behind Taipei’s two-Michelin-starred Sushi Amamoto—a reservation so notoriously tough to secure that die-hard sushi-heads are known to blueprint trips to Taiwan around it. (Sushi mastery clearly runs in the family: his brother, Masamichi, helms Tokyo’s cult-favorite Higashiazabu Amamoto.) Chef Shogo’s London outpost forgoes the usual Mayfair glitz in favor of a serene, minimalist room centered around a pale hinoki wood counter and bespoke Japanese ceramics, and the focus lies firmly in classic Edomae culinary craft. Dishes feature top-tier seafood flown in from Tokyo’s Toyosu Market alongside standout European catches—translucent slices of French wild seabass sashimi with shiso flower and ponzu, a sweet seared Orkney scallop wrapped in crisp nori, or rich, smoky nodoguro whose skin crackles straight off the grill—and warm, perfectly seasoned rice. It’s purist without feeling oppressively solemn—and one of the freshest (in every sense) newly introduced additions to London’s luxury sushi roster. —L.H.

One of London’s sexiest counter seats (and that’s saying something), Ushio arrives from Fukuoka, on Japan’s Kyushu island. Its first European location, Ushio serves A5 wagyu omakase style (no sushi here!), specifically akami wagyu that has been imported from Japan. It’s leaner and higher in protein, with a taste that will unfurl across an incisive multi-course menu of wagyu every which way. You’ll get a card that tells you which prime cut of beef you’re eating with every course, and it’s certainly a journey. Some are barely kissed by the grill, others draped in a rich sukiyaki marinade or glazed in their signature tare sauce. A trio of tenderloin, tongue, and kurimi are delicately salted and presented gloriously as is. (My tip? Say yes to the extra curry course! If it wasn’t so sophisticated in there, I would be licking the bowl. Add the sake pairing and enjoy your time with the very charming sommelier too.) Finish with a (meatless, but still mighty) matcha choux puff. In a quiet, darkened corridor of Fitzrovia, the minimal interiors are stunning and sleek, just like the Fukuoka flagship, built around wood and stone with Ko-Imari porcelains and hand-built ceramics by Taeko Kajihara. And everyone who works there just seems cool! A spot that lingers long on the palate. —A.C.

Tucked behind a bright white storefront in Clerkenwell, this seven-person omakase experience is among the city’s toughest reservations to secure. Husband-and-wife duo Harumi and Toru Takahashi are behind the operation (the latter being the chef), both of whom are famously warm and welcoming, fostering a convivial atmosphere versus the buttoned-up formality of traditional omakase settings. The seasonal menu relies on what is strongest in the market that day, but expect sushi so fresh it melts in your mouth and impeccable sake pairings. The restaurant sits along Jerusalem Passage, an 18th-century path to the priory of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem, which later transformed into a pedestrian walkway linking St John’s Square to Aylesbury Street. —Nicole Kliest.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re craving sushi but aren’t in the mood for a formal omakase environment, Uchi Hackney achieves an exceptional balance. This ultra-cozy spot in a residential area of Hackney leans on traditional Japanese design motifs (linen, ceramics, wood), and even encourages guests to kick off their shoes and slip into a pair of provided slippers. The restaurant began as a delivery service in 2015 and now offers a high-quality menu in its brick-and-mortar location, serving both brunch and dinner. As for the dishes, expect a variety of hot favorites such as grilled pork belly skewers and lightly deep-fried tofu, and savor the selection of fresh sushi and sake to round out the experience. (An aside: Uchi Hackney’s intimate ambience makes for the perfect date night locale.) —N.K.

It has been revealed that set on the ninth-floor Liverpool Street branch of Los Mochis, arriving at Luna Omakase comes with a delightful sense of ceremony. As the evening begins, you’ll be guided with your group from the bar along a nondescript corridor to a set of sliding doors that are opened—with plenty of theatrical flourish—to reveal the 12-seater dining room, where a sculptural timber counter is lit with a lunar glow against a backdrop of glittering skyline views of the City. Over the course of 12 seasonal plates, the vibe is lively and conversational, as the sushi masters hand each pristine slice of aged fish—think melt-in-your-mouth otoro tartare with Oscietra caviar served with a cloud of smoke, or juicy king crab leg nigiri with feathery shavings of yuzu—and artfully balance traditional technique and off-the-cuff flourishes throughout the meal. (If you fancy it, you can also make the evening more spirited—quite literally—courtesy of the tightly curated list of rare sakes and Japanese whiskies that the team is more than happy to geek out over, and that will serve as an instant conversation starter with your fellow sushi obsessives.) It’s intimate and undeniably stylish, but free of the stuffiness that can make your typical high-end omakase experience feel a little intimidating. —L.H.

Industry observers note that in operation for nearly 30 years, this beloved sushi institution now operates across eight outposts in London (plus six in Tokyo). For those who favor great value and generous portion sizes, this restaurant chain consistently gets top marks. Choose from a menu of sushi, sashimi, nigiri, chirashi, unagi, or opt for a bento box to get the full experience. Their latest creation worth dining out for? Wagyu with black tobiko (or a ‘sushi taco’, as it’s so nicknamed). —N.K.

This Japanese udon noodle bar opened its doors in Soho back in 2010 and has since expanded to three popular London locations, plus a shop offering provisions such as chilli oil and jars of Fukujinzuke. The original location is worth a visit for the freshly made noodles and dashi alone, but don’t sleep on the weekly blackboard specials either (previous highlights include grilled corn with miso butter and fried whitebait with shibazuke cucumber). Koya Soho is walk-ins only and is open from breakfast through to dinner. —N.K.

This is where you go when you want authentic Japanese food and a killer sake selection, all in a calm, relaxed setting. Chisou’s two central London locations—Mayfair and Knightsbridge—treat guests to seasonally changing dishes and a menu of wow-worthy raw fish, with the option to sit at a sushi bar or at an intimate table. And back to the sake for a moment: Chisou prides itself on having one of the largest menus around, with experts on hand to suggest pairings and special events like sake and British cheese pairing classes led by specialists. —N.K.

In a recent development, A charming, intimate spot tucked away on Newly introduced Quebec Street in Marylebone, Roketsu recently relaunched as a rare example in London of kappo-style dining, where the chefs will whip up a customized set menu based on a conversation about your preferences at the beginning of the meal. The team of chefs here take a creative approach to classic Japanese cuisine, folding in a handful of French flourishes: most notably, perhaps, with one of the restaurant’s signature dishes, an opening bite of a crisp wafer filled with 10-day miso-marinated foie gras. (Other highlights included Cornish cod with a vibrant nori sauce, and flame-grilled wagyu beef with yuzu oroshi for a clean, citrus-forward finish.) With an open kitchen behind a hinoki wood counter, Roketsu is an elevated, classically Japanese dining experience—but it also comes with an element of choose-your-own-adventure fun that makes it feel genuinely unique. —L.H.

If you’re seeking a quirkier spin on omakase dining, head over to Notting Hill, where you’ll find the six-seat Juno hidden in a speakeasy-like space at the back of Los Mochis, the popular neighborhood Mexican-Japanese restaurant on Uxbridge St. The dining room’s delightfully funky, “Tokyo-meets-Tulum” decor—bamboo, seagrass, high-gloss wallpaper—should serve as an initial clue for what to expect here: the textures and flavors of Japanese cuisine are lent a fresh twist courtesy of a bold, Mexican-inspired toolkit of spices, acids, and smoke. (Think chutoro spiked with a sharp kick of fermented jalapeño, or red bream brushed with lime aioli and topped with a sprinkle of crushed-up Oaxacan flying ant for a surprisingly delicious note of nutty earthiness.) Bring your friends and make it a party. —L.H.

In a recent development, there are few more scenic spots for lunchtime sushi in London than chef Endo Kazutoshi’s rooftop restaurant, which sits proudly above the Raffles London hotel at the Old War Office—and trades the monastic restraint of Endo’s Michelin-starred White City flagship for sweeping views over Horse Guards Parade. Grab an outdoor table and browse a menu that bridges Japanese precision with Mediterranean flourishes, the latter a direct nod to the years Kazutoshi spent cooking in Spain. Most of the dishes are built for sharing, so order generously: try the tuna tartare on miso brioche, the yellowfin tuna “chorizo” (its smoky, paprika-laced punch is balanced by pickled tsukemono and warm pita), or the charred, melt-in-the-mouth octopus with miso, fava beans, and asakura sansho—it’s all rather decadent, but somehow never overly heavy. Come for the pristine, perfectly seasoned nigiri; stay for the golden-hour sunset over the Neoclassical rooftops of this stately corner of central London. —L.H.

Many of the best Japanese restaurants fall into two categories: no-frills neighborhood ramen and udon spots, or the kind of hushed, six-seater omakase counters where you might be frowned at for asking for extra soy sauce. Aki London, tucked inside a soaring, Grade II-listed former bank on Cavendish Square, couldn’t be more different. Designed by Francis Sultana, the dining room is all about pure, flamboyant glamour—think fluted marble columns, soaring coffered ceilings, and plush velvet banquette seating. This isn’t a case of style over substance, however: The kitchen leans into farm-to-table Japanese cooking rooted in Kyoto traditions, ranging from crisp, featherlight tempura rock shrimp to delicate steamed-and-crisped wagyu gyoza, to smoky, tare-brushed chicken thigh skewers straight off the robata grill. Whether you’re coming for a leisurely lunch or a late-night dinner, make sure to check out the subterranean cocktail bar first for a round of yuzu-infused martinis. (Aki is best enjoyed in the firm of a lively group.) —L.H.

Industry observers note that A neighborhood restaurant in the truest sense, Jin Kichi’s cult following makes booking a table a competitive sport. This tiny, two-floor restaurant is cozy, often crowded, and wonderfully authentic. While the yakitori is a major draw, the sushi and sashimi are of a quality that rivals the city’s most expensive counters. It’s the kind of place where the chefs know the regulars by name (and where noted regulars might be the likes of Kate Moss and Harry Styles). —L.H.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that growing up, my dad did all of his holiday shopping on Christmas Eve (and still largely does), which gave me anxiety and turned me into the person who gets all shopping done well before December 1. As a collector myself, I like to gift Lego sets because a) there’s legitimately a set for everyone, and b) I want everyone to love Lego as much as I do. I will not rest until they do.

Sources indicate that ‘Tis the season to sparkle, and that includes makeup too. Glitter eyeshadow? Check. A sparkly lipstick? Done! Shimmering cheeks? You got it! Glitter makeup is currently taking over the holiday season and we’re here for it.

It has been revealed that gone are the days when glitter meant a chunky, craft-store mess that followed you home from the party (and highlighted up in your bed a week later). Today’s formulas are finer, smoother, and far more wearable, with ultra-fine particles, gel and liquid bases that grip the skin, and pressed pigments that deliver a high-shine finish without the fallout. Whether you’re dressing up for an office party, a New Year’s Eve countdown, or simply want your everyday look to catch the twinkle lights, there’s a glittery option made for you.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best glitter makeup, from an easy-to-apply wash of shimmer on the lids to full-on disco-ball glam. Consider this your shortlist for holiday party season.

Bring on the ethereal shine with Dior’s Glazed Violet lipstick. Available in two dazzling shades, it adds a touch of sparkle to your look without going overboard.

Half Magic's glitter pots are highly rated for their showstopping sparkle. Dubbed "grown-up" glitter, they deliver high-impact shine in a refined, wearable formula that's easy to apply and built to last through the party.

With a high percentage of reflective pearls, this baked highlighter is a silky, buildable formula that melts into the skin for a luminous, lit-from-within glow. Sweep it on lightly for a soft, dewy sheen, or layer it up for a high-impact, party-ready shine on the cheekbones, brow bones, and Cupid’s bow.

The glitter body gel from the early aughts, redefined for this new era of sparkle. With a blend of multidimensional, multicolored glitters, this mess-free gel is ready to be applied anywhere on your face or body, whether you’re dabbing it on the lids, tracing it along your collarbones, or going all-out from head to toe.

Sources indicate that for a megawatt look that can be spotted from across the room, this high-shine glitter delivers intense sparkle with a single swipe. The satiny, fast-setting formula grips the skin for all-night wear, so you can go from the first toast to the last dance without a touch-up.

With a creamy, blendable formula, these shimmer stick shadows deliver easy, instant application. They’re waterproof, transfer-proof, and crease-proof: the triple threat we all dream of with glitter eyeshadow.

With a sheer wash of color, this glimmering lip oil delivers a veil of hydration alongside the prettiest, most delicate sheen. The high-shine finish comes with a non-sticky formula, making it a holiday-season staple worthy of your everyday beauty rotation.

Liquid glitter eyeliner is a game changer when it comes to glitter eye makeup. With a precise brush tip and a formula that dries down fast, it lets you trace a sparkling wing, line the waterline's edge, or add a flash of shimmer to the inner corners without the mess of loose glitter.

It’s all shine and shimmer with this glitzy eyeshadow palette. Pairing warm and cool tones, it's a versatile go-to for holiday parties and beyond.

The easiest way to wear glitter this season: a liquid formula that melts onto lids for a smooth, dazzling finish.

According to recent reports, this creamy lipstick in Rose Quartz is pearl-infused and gives a metallic shine rather than a glittery one, delivering a soft, light-catching finish that looks polished from the first coat. #157875. Latest Update: The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

Latest Update: The 20 Most Iconic Colognes of All Time, According to GQ in 2026

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece.
  • All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years.
  • According to recent reports, our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the first notes of The Beach Boys’ God Only Knows are enough to understand you're listening to a masterpiece. Well, as a longtime fragrance editor, I get a similar feeling when I smell Guerlain’s iconic Vétiver scent (or, more recently, Penhaligon’s Halfeti). These fragrances smelled exceptional when they debuted, still do today, probably still will a hundred years from now. And while fragrance, like any art form, has its trends, the truly great scents (and songs) have a way of deflecting them and singing on.

All of this is why we wanted to take a moment to celebrate not only the colognes our editors are wearing today, but also the fragrances that have been enjoyed by millions of GQ readers over the years. To do so, I dug through the history of men’s fragrance to put together a list of some of the most iconic colognes of all time. Scents that defined an era, changed the course of perfumery, or smelled so good that folks never stopped wearing them.

According to recent reports, our criteria came down to three things: legacy, or how a fragrance helped shape the scent landscape; longevity, meaning it has remained relevant or recognizable; and wearability, because the best classics should (mostly) still smell great today, not just serve as nostalgic reminders of another time. You might love some more than others, but all have earned their place in the fragrance pantheon. Here are 20 of the most popular, influential, and enduring colognes ever made, and exactly why they’ve lasted.

Is there a more classic cologne than Acqua di Parma’s Colonia? Launched in 1916, this timeless citrus is the original Italian splash, and it would be criminal not to include it on a list of this caliber. That crisp, bright citrus opening is unmistakable, but there’s so much more going on beneath the surface as it dries down, with the supporting notes weaving in and out without ever stealing the show. Herbaceous hints of lavender and rosemary add herbal hues, while earthy vetiver and patchouli mingle with the smooth warmth of sandalwood as it settles on the skin. This is one of the great daily drivers, if not the very archetype of what an everyday cologne could or should be. It’s a 10/10 blend of citrus, aromatics, and woods, and more than a century on, still smells as sophisticated as ever.

It has been revealed that I’ve written about Guerlain Vétiver so many times, you’d think I’d have run out of ways to sing its praises. But I could go forever. Few fragrances have done more to establish vetiver as a leading note, and since its 1959 debut, this masterpiece has remained every bit as relevant and wearable. It beautifully captures vetiver’s fresher, greener side, rather than leaning into its smoky, earthy character. There’s a crispness, with bright citrus, a touch of spice, and grassy vetiver balanced by subtle tobacco and woods, like the first cool, earthy dew on a spring morning. Elegant and confident, it oozes the kind of sophistication I imagine old-school Hollywood leading men appreciating, yet it wears just as well today, whether you're suited up or simply going about your day.

Sources indicate that ask me to name the most influential luxury fragrance of the 21st century, and there’s a good chance I’d say Aventus (notice, I said “luxury”). I’ve seen firsthand just how many guys made their first foray into high-end fragrance with this icon, and while I now often gravitate toward some of the deeper cuts in Creed’s storied catalog, every time I wear Aventus, the compliments roll in. Since its 2010 debut, it has inspired countless imitators and the inevitable fragrance fatigue that comes with being a phenomenon, yet I don’t think it’s lost an ounce of its appeal. To me, it's the ultimate wedding fragrance, a perfect blend of bright citrus and pineapple, aromatic freshness, and rich, smoky woods that’s refined without being fussy. The defining fragrance of the 2010s? I’d make that argument any day. Aventus will always have a place on my shelf.

No. 89 is one of the great British gentlemen’s fragrances, and few colognes capture Bond-like elegance quite like it. And it tracks: Introduced in 1951, No. 89 counted James Bond creator Ian Fleming among its famous admirers, while Cary Grant and Sir Alec Guinness were reportedly devotees as well. The scent itself is traditional in the best way, a classically composed fougère with crisp, almost barbershop-like citrus and lavender freshness, subtle florals, warming spice, and a smooth, woody base of vetiver and oakmoss. Aromatic, gently spicy, and impeccably polished, it’s the olfactory equivalent of a beautifully tailored Savile Row suit. More than seven decades on, No. 89 is proof that class and character never go out of style.

Industry observers note that back in the ’90s, CK One was everywhere. From Wall Street execs to flannel-wearing creatives; its intoxicating freshness just captured the zeitgeist. It was also one of the first mainstream fragrances marketed as unisex. (Almost an afterthought for fragrance fans today, it was a fairly novel concept then.) And while countless fragrances have followed in its footsteps, this citrusy, green, woodsy, lightly sweet profile still more than holds up. A surprising amount is going on here, too: a bright medley of citrus and tropical fruits, a floral heart with hints of spice, and a clean, musky base of cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s an icon that helped define a generation, and it works just as well day or night, on pretty much anyone. And perhaps most impressively, after all these years, CK One still smells unmistakably like CK One.

Much like his clothing, Ralph Lauren’s original Polo fragrance has left an indelible mark on American style. Introduced in 1978, the unmistakable green-bottled cologne helped define what a classic masculine fragrance could smell like: sophisticated, confident, and unapologetically aromatic. And while nearly five decades have passed, there’s still nothing quite like it. That signature pine-heavy character is front and center, surrounded by a rich blend of herb and spices with bergamot adding brightness and leather lending rugged, earthy depth. It’s bold, woody, green, and distinctly old-school, but that’s precisely its charm. It’s undergone reformulations over the years, and its assertive character won’t appeal to everyone, but there’s no denying its place in the fragrance hall of fame. Some colognes come and go, but Polo isn’t going anywhere.

Recent findings suggest that when I spotted that frosted bottle in my dad’s medicine cabinet and wore it for the first time, I had no idea that this scent would spark a lifelong fragrance obsession. Armani’s 1996 icon, Acqua di Giò, has been worn by millions, referenced endlessly, and spawned countless flankers, but the original remains one of those rare mass-appeal designer colognes that have stood the test of time. Why? Because it’s just so wearable. Long before the niche fragrance boom, when designer colognes dominated department store counters, Acqua di Giò caught on like wildfire, appealing to just about every kind of guy, whether for the office or date night. At its core is a beautifully nuanced blend of citrus, fresh marine accords, and soft florals, grounded by a musky amber base. On skin, it’s breezy, clean, and subtly woody, with an oceanic quality. If you’ve never rocked it or haven’t reached for it in years, do yourself a favor and revisit this classic.

In a recent development, imitation is the highest form of flattery, and so many colognes still try to smell like Cool Water. Released in 1988, it became a full-blown phenomenon in the ’90s, and for a generation of guys, it was practically a rite of passage. Along with CK One, it was non-negotiable during my formative years, and even then, before I’d developed my own distinct taste, I knew I didn’t want to smell like everyone else. But there was something about this intoxicating green aquatic I just couldn’t resist. Its blend of lavender, mint, rosemary, and neroli nodded to classic gentleman’s fougères, but Cool Water took that aromatic DNA somewhere newly introduced—a singular scent that’s herbal and richly marine, softened by a woody, musky warmth. While it might smell dated to some, there’s no denying its place among the most iconic fragrances of all time, and I’d argue it still smells amazing on the right dude, especially on a spring or summer day.

Terre d’Hermès is (probably) my favorite designer fragrance of all time. When Jean-Claude Ellena created it back in 2006, he delivered something entirely different from the crowd-pleasing designer colognes of the day. There’s an earthiness to it that I find irresistible, a marriage of citrus, dry woods, spice, and that unmistakable flinty, mineral character that gives it so much personality. It’s sophisticated without being stuffy, with a gorgeous, almost boozy warmth that makes it feel sultry and downright sexy. I particularly love wearing it in colder weather, when those warm, woody facets really come alive, but I can reach for it almost anytime. Plenty of designer colognes are simply pleasant, but Terre d’Hermès is distinctive and endlessly wearable.

Few colognes in modern history have generated as much conversation, inspired as many memes, or become quite as zeitgeist-y as Dior Sauvage. Love it or roll your eyes at its popularity, its influence on modern men’s perfumery is undeniable. Since its debut in 2015, Sauvage has become one of the world’s bestselling fragrances, at times even claiming the number-one spot. And it’s easy to see why. That unmistakable blend of citrus, spice, and all things ambery nice is crisp and fresh, with a warm, woody drydown that’s oh so smooth. It’s a crowd-pleaser in the truest sense, versatile enough to wear just about anywhere, though I think it really shines after dark. Sauvage has since spawned an entire family of flankers, but the original EDT started it all.

You've smelled Bleu de Chanel on plenty of guys. A beautifully composed citrus-spice-wood classic, it works just as well with a navy suit as it does with a white tee and jeans. Note: When Chanel's legendary perfumer Jacques Polge introduced it in 2010, he didn't just create another handsome, crowd-pleasing cologne; he helped define the modern blue fragrance, a fresh, clean, citrusy, and woody genre that's become a mainstay. Sixteen years on, the original remains one of the most approachable and endlessly versatile colognes ever. Its bright citrus opening gives way to an aromatic blend of cool mint, warming spices, and subtle florals, all grounded by a rich, woody base with touches of earthy vetiver, patchouli, and resinous warmth. There really is only one Bleu.

Recent findings suggest that this was a tough call. Ask any scent head about Tom Ford's fragrances, and they’ll surely bring up Neroli Portofino and Tobacco Vanille, both arguably just as iconic (and good) as this one. But if you polled fans on the most influential Tom Ford fragrances, I think Oud Wood would edge out the competition. Launched in 2007, it helped introduce Oud to a broader Western audience, making the traditionally intense ingredient feel approachable. It’s elegant and beautifully blended, with a smoky, almost creamy heart of oud, sandalwood, and rosewood, accented by subtle spice and the warmth of vanilla and amber. It’s heady yet easy to wear, with an addictive richness that never wears thin.

I’ve worn pretty much every Le Labo under the sun, and while my personal favorites lean toward the eucalyptus and vetiver side of the house, there’s simply no telling the story of modern perfumery without Santal 33. Love it or find it utterly overplayed, you’ve smelled it. Since its 2011 debut, it’s wafted through elevators, the backseats of cabs, countless weddings and date nights, and just about everywhere in between. More importantly, it helped bring sandalwood into the mainstream, and became a reference point for an entire genre of warm, woody fragrances. But before everyone started rocking it, Santal 33 was, and still is, a brilliant composition: creamy sandalwood, dry cedar, cardamom spice, and leathery warmth. It’s a niche legend that has suffered from its own success, yes, but give it another ten years, and don’t be surprised if the very fragrance many got tired of smelling becomes cool all over again.

If you’re remotely a scent head, chances are you dig at least one, if not several, of Parfums de Marly’s fragrances (my personal favorite is the oud-praline magic that is Haltane). But if I had to sum up the house in one word, it would be regal. It does refined, layered elegance exceptionally well, and while some folks might champion Althaïr or Castley, to my nose, the fougère-forward Layton best epitomizes the house. Rolled out in 2016, it’s one of the finest fougères I’ve ever smelled, rich yet airy, with classic lavender reimagined alongside crisp apple, bright citrus, cardamom, woods, and a healthy dose of vanilla. It’s practically the template for what a modern fougère aspires to be, and its enduring popularity suggests plenty of fragrance fans would agree. It doesn’t hurt that the matte blue bottle with its signature silver dome is so flauntworthy.

Recent findings suggest that few fragrances in recent times have had the same cultural impact as Baccarat Rouge 540, becoming a signature scent for everyone from socialites to fragrance obsessives. Yes, it's polarizing, and some might argue its ubiquity has stripped it of some of its magic. But it's become a modern classic for a reason, starting with the masterful nose behind it: Francis Kurkdjian, founder of his namesake maison. Launched in 2015, it's a luminous floral amber, with saffron lending spice, jasmine bringing a soft warmth, and a generous dose of amberwood creating that glowing aura. Sultry, heady, and diffusive, it's a straight-up unisex phenomenon that smells a little different on everyone who wears it, yet still announces itself before you even enter a room. Whether you're a devotee or a detractor, there's no denying it's left its mark.

Recent findings suggest that it came down to Bal d’Afrique and Gypsy Water, though plenty of Byredo fragrances could have earned a spot here. But I’m the editor, and I’m going with my all-time favorite from one of the houses that helped bring niche perfumery into the mainstream. Introduced in 2008, Gypsy Water was one of the first niche fragrances I ever fell for, and it holds such a special place in my heart that I still wear it regularly. There’s something almost holy about its airy blend of incense, soft woods, bright lemon, and a whisper of vanilla and amber, all coming together with that subtle yet magnetic, almost skin-scent quality Byredo does so well. Artsy, chic, and easy to love, this woody aromatic never tries too hard to make an impression yet often leaves a lasting one.

Since its 2015 debut, Xerjoff’s Naxos has achieved near-mythic status, winning over everyone from fragrance-obsessed TikTokers to yacht-owning gentlemen with decidedly expensive taste. And I get it. This is an almost impossibly well-blended composition that somehow manages to be both decadent and incredibly wearable, making it a great place to start if you’re looking to venture into niche perfumery. On paper, the combination of tobacco, aromatic lavender, fruity freshness, and a prominent honey accord sounds like it shouldn’t quite work, but man, does it ever. That rich sweetness is a defining feature, especially in the opening, before the herbal, earthy tones and a hefty dose of vanilla come together in a downright sumptuous yet crisp way. The hype may have quieted down since its social media heyday, but Naxos deserves its flowers as a modern niche standout.

Halfeti has become a signature of mine, though I’m admittedly a little late to the game, having received my first bottle as a birthday gift last year, well after it had achieved iconic status in scent circles. But better late than never, especially when a fragrance is this good. Named after a Turkish town known for its roses, it leans into a rich, heady floral style, layered with citrus, herbs, and spice. Bergamot and grapefruit lift the opening before saffron and cardamom give way to a deep base of leather, oud, cedar, sandalwood, and amber. It’s a lot, but it all hangs together gorgeously, creating a woody, spicy, aromatic scent that’s elegant and sexy, perfect for special occasions or date nights. But I’d happily wear it just about anywhere, including when I’m not going anywhere at all.

Musc Ravageur embodies the risk-taking spirit of niche perfumery. Introduced in 2000, it helped redefine what a modern musk fragrance could be at a time when fresh, clean fragrances dominated the men’s market. More than a quarter century later, it remains a cult favorite, thanks in no small part to its warm, almost funky (in a good way) richness. It opens with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and rose, all resting on a base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. A benchmark for animalic musks, it’s an alluring, sultry, and unapologetically sensual aroma, equally suited to being a signature scent or an olfactory companion for wherever the evening leads.

Amouage has dropped so many olfactory bangers over the years that choosing just one for this list wasn't easy. The Omani house has built its reputation on rich, complex compositions that keep you coming back to sniff your pulse points, and while I could make a case for several of its fragrances, Reflection Man feels quintessentially Amouage. Introduced in 2007, it’s become a luxury niche benchmark, proving that a floral-forward fragrance can be every bit as rich and sophisticated as its woody or spicy counterparts. It opens with an herbaceous blend of rosemary, berries, and orange before orris, jasmine, and ylang-ylang bring a lush, earthy depth, all grounded by a smooth base of vetiver, patchouli, and sandalwood. The result is a layered floral-woody scent that’s distinctive without being difficult to wear, and versatile enough for everything from a boardroom to a black-tie gala. Pricey, yes, but worth every spritz.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Friday is officially here—and whether or not you made it through the roster of early sales that broke last week, it’s time to reap the benefits of waiting for the main event. With fresh discounts, deeper markdowns, and plenty of coveted finds now up for grabs, there’s no shortage of pieces worth adding to your cart today. With so much to sift through, I always like to start with recommendations from my fellow Vogue editors for inspiration.

This year, the deeper discounts are calling—and Vogue shopping editors are finally pulling the trigger on the pieces they’ve been eyeing all season. From luxe outerwear and cozy cold-weather accessories to covetable footwear (think elevated mules, sleek leather boots, and everyday loafers), plus loads of chic home and beauty finds. These wish lists are filled with all manner of luxuries, both substantial and small, at the best prices of the season.

Industry observers note that I myself am grabbing a few fall wardrobe heroes—from Arma’s sumptuous suede blazer to Khaite’s deep indigo denim and A.Emery’s little black sock boots that go with just about everything. Why wait when some of the best pieces are finally within reach?

Consider this your inside look at what’s actually worth adding to your cart this Black Friday, as our team continues to scout the standout deals and wish-list-worthy pieces worth shopping through the Cyber sale weekend.

According to recent reports, “I discovered heaps of floaty nightgowns at Dôen—they may not be seasonally appropriate, but they are on sale. I wear my wool mockneck from 440me nearly weekly at home. I have it in the camel color but am eyeing the white now that it’s on sale, as well as their black boatneck wool-silk shirt. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that perhaps it never occurred to you that you might need a list of the best nose hair trimmers until this very moment.
  • Sources indicate that similar to other battery-operated beard trimmers, back shavers, razors, hair clippers, or body hair trimmers, these trimmers are ergonomic and designed with durability in mind.
  • If you’re looking for a quick, pain-free way to get rid of unwanted nose whiskers, Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer Series 5000 can absolutely handle that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that perhaps it never occurred to you that you might need a list of the best nose hair trimmers until this very moment. Fear not—reasonably priced, speedily shipped (thanks, Amazon), simple-to-use options populate this list of our favorites. Meaning—whenever you have a general facial hair emergency that calls for rogue hair removal, you need not add an ear hair trimmer or brow trimmer to your cart. You need only think back to this moment and thank your lucky stars for choosing a gadget to cut hair—wherever it may appear.

Sources indicate that similar to other battery-operated beard trimmers, back shavers, razors, hair clippers, or body hair trimmers, these trimmers are ergonomic and designed with durability in mind. You can use many of them on wet or dry hair to trim nose hair, and like other electric razors you may be familiar with, most can actually be used for nose & ears (and also as eyebrow trimmers).

If you’re looking for a quick, pain-free way to get rid of unwanted nose whiskers, Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer Series 5000 can absolutely handle that. But this versatile grooming device also covers most hair-detailing needs with precision and gusto. Add in the affordable price, and that’s why it stands as our pick for the best nose hair trimmer, bar none.

The 5000 Series includes three types of trimmers: a linear-style trimmer, plus the rotary and detail attachments. Depending on your preference, you can use either the linear or rotary trimmer for both nose and ear hairs as well as working as an eyebrow trimmer. Personally, I appreciate the size of the cylinder on the rotary trimmer, which is wider than most and is able to capture overgrown hairs better than any other trimmer I tested. The linear trimmer works great at managing eyebrows (thanks to two different guard lengths) and tending to fuzzy ear canals. Perhaps the unsung hero of the kit is the straight-edge detail trimmer, which is more than capable of daily touch-ups. Think sideburns, mustaches, or even edging beards in a pinch.

The 5000 Series is battery-powered, cordless, easy to wash with a rinse in the bathroom sink, and you already know that anything made from Philips Norelco has longevity. If what you’re after is a no-frills device to manage most facial hair needs, consider this trimmer twenty bucks well spent. Adam Hurly.

True to its name, Wahl’s Micro Groomsman is easily the smallest nose hair trimmer we recommend—but don’t let its diminutive size fool you. This is a perfectly pared-down trimmer that’s great for home use, and even better for travel. Heck, it’s so small you might forget you stashed it in your dopp kit.

Sources indicate that the Micro Groomsman offers two interchangeable heads, including a rotary trimmer for nose and ears, and a linear trimmer for detailed work. You can also attach an eyebrow guard to manage any overgrown caterpillars up top. The compact design feels great in the hand, and the stainless steel blades are cinch to clean. Even if you have a primary grooming device you love, we readily recommend the Wahl Micro Groomsman as a go-to backup option or a permanent accessory in your travel kit. Adam Hurly.

In a recent development, got a partner who absolutely hates when you leave trimmed hair in the sink? This one’s for you. An upgrade from the standard Panasonic ER-GN30 (shown in the video), this trimmer offers everything you’d want from a dedicated nose hair trimmer, but what sets it apart is a vacuum system that sucks up clippings in an instant. Easy clean-up, yes, but the vacuum system also helps prevent bacteria build-up. We call that a win-win.

Recent findings suggest that otherwise, this tool is fairly minimal with no fancy attachments. You get a rotary trimmer, and that’s all. Granted, it’s a powerful one that’s able to mow down the coarsest strands. All told, the GN70-K is best for the person who just needs a dependable nose and ear trimmer that will save them from the mess. Adam Hurly.

A whole grooming kit is excessive if all you need to tackle is the occasional nose hair. But if you’re also maintaining a beard, tidying body hair, or cutting your own hair, Philips’ 9000 starts to make much more sense. The current kit has 23 tools and accessories, including a nose and ear head, with a stainless-steel handle and rubber grip. Philips rates it for up to six hours between charges.

Long-term testing notes: Philips' previous iteration of the Multigroom 9000 was my go-to grooming tool. Alas, I only realized how much I relied on its nose hair shaving attachment after I lost the thing. Now there's a latest (albeit broadly similar) enhancement of the same device, and I'm back to trimming as much hair as humanly possible with one device. My advice for anyone else who picks up this trimmer? Be sure to check every piece when packing up after a trip. Adam Hurly.

It has been revealed that my nose hairs have become alarmingly ambitious with age, which is unfortunate given how little enthusiasm I have for plucking, waxing, or the local Turkish barber’s fire tricks. The Weed Whacker 3.0 Pro, thankfully, gets the job done with considerably less drama. Alongside its rotary nose and ear head, there’s a separate eyebrow blade with a 2mm comb. USB-C charging saves another proprietary cable, and the travel lock stops it switching on in your bag.

Industry observers note that long-term testing notes: During my review testing, the rotary head cut through my thick, wiry hairs promptly, without the pulling and sneezing fits I’ve experienced with cheaper trimmers. It was still ticklish, but the compact head was easy to maneuver around my nostrils and ears. The LED helped in my dimly lit bathroom, showing hairs I might otherwise have missed. I also liked the solid-feeling matte-black handle and how easily it rinsed clean. The claimed hour of runtime held up in testing, too. It’s the best dedicated nose trimmer I’ve used. Esat Dedezade.

According to recent reports, if you have a beard and your grooming routine requires a more exacting tool, ConairMan’s Nose and Ear Trimmer kit will serve you well. I think of this more as a mustache and beard-line tidier-upper, as opposed to a nose hair trimmer.

Sources indicate that the tool has a rotary blade that makes quick work of nostril hairs. But its two-faced trimming and shaving head is its best calling card—you get a straight-edge detailer on one side, and a shaver on the other. If you’re looking for a tool that can truly tend to the lower half of your face, ConairMan offers an excellent package that’ll get the job done. Adam Hurly.

Philips’ 7000 costs less than the 9000 above and still covers far more than nose hair. The US kit includes 22 tools and accessories, with a precision comb for short facial hair and heads for wider grooming jobs. Finding somewhere to keep all those small parts is part of the deal.

My main complaint, as always, is the proprietary charging connection. The supplied cable plugs into USB-A at the other end, but you still need Philips’ cable to charge the trimmer. Braun, Remington, and other brands are just as guilty of this, by the way.

According to recent reports, long-term testing notes: In my three-week test of the 7000, its nose and ear attachment cut comfortably without pulling, snagging, or irritation. It was much less unpleasant than plucking. The wider kit also earned its place on my chest and underarms, so the extra attachments felt useful. Esat Dedezade.

It has been revealed that if you already have a Panasonic MultiShape, the nose-trimming head gives its rechargeable handle another job. It swaps with the system’s beard trimmer, shaver, and toothbrush heads, so there’s one less complete gadget to pack when you travel.

According to recent reports, for a new buyer, the lithium-ion handle and nose head cost around $81.99 together. The $21.99 attachment won’t work on its own, and the other heads cost extra. That makes the MultiShape easier to justify if you’ll use more of the system. For nose hair alone, a dedicated trimmer is a simpler buy.

Long-term testing notes: During several weeks with a broader MultiShape kit, I found the nose head cleared unwanted hair without pain or friction. The lightweight handle was comfortable, and switching from trimming to shaving or brushing his teeth took little effort. That ease of moving between jobs made the system particularly useful for travel. The handle and nose head linked here are sold separately from the other attachments he used. Owen Gough.

While many nose hair trimmers tout motors with serious RPMs and boast about their long battery life, the truth is, you won’t be using it much—maybe once every couple weeks for a mere 5 or 10 seconds. But that’s no excuse to skimp on them, either. Here are a few things to consider:.

According to recent reports, we’ve tested all manner of nose hair trimmers for this guide, from simple battery-powered models to grooming kits with interchangeable heads. We look at how comfortably they cut, whether they pull or miss hairs, and how easy they are to handle and clean. Extra attachments need to be useful, and we consider battery life and charging alongside performance.

The guide draws on Adam Hurly’s years of grooming reviews and Ian Burke’s experience of living with the Zorami trimmer long after receiving it as a joke gift. My additions bring in testing for British GQ, alongside Owen Gough’s assessment of the MultiShape system. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation. You can read more about our editorial standards at About GQ.

What is the best nose hair trimmer?

Sources indicate that the best men’s nose hair trimmer is Philips Norelco’s Nose Trimmer 5000 Series, according to GQ. The powerful device offers dual trimming options (for internal and peripheral nostril hairs) and also functions as a facial hair, eyebrow, and ear hair trimmer.

Can a nose hair trimmer cut you?

Sources indicate that whether you are using a rotary head or a linear head, nose hair trimmers are built with a protective guard, which ensures the blade doesn’t come in direct contact with the skin. The protective guard also helps you get a clean cut so the device doesn’t pull or pluck at your nose hairs. Generally speaking, nose hair trimmers do not hurt.

Not only can nose hair trimmers be washed, but it is important to disinfect them between use, first by flushing out stray hair clippings. Let them dry before storing, too, to avoid rust and bacterial proliferation between each use. It’s a good idea to clean the device again before using it, since it is going into your nose, after all.

Do you need a nose hair trimmer, and how often should you use it?

If visible nose hairs bother you, a trimmer is a simple way to keep them tidy. There’s no fixed schedule to follow – a quick trim when hairs start showing is usually all that’s needed. Concentrate on those visible hairs around the nostril opening, rather than trying to remove everything inside. Ear hair and eyebrows can be tidied as needed, using the appropriate attachment and comb.

How do you use a nose hair trimmer?

To trim your nose hair, simply stick the trimming tip of the device in your nostril and apply a gentle circular motion. Here are a few more tips to keep in mind, according to Simone:.

How do I clean my nose hair trimmer?

In a recent development, the cleaning systems for nose hair trimmers vary. “Some nose hair trimmers are waterproof, so it’s easy to just rinse under water, if you are the sole user, and just let it air dry,” claims Simone. If you share the device with somebody else, then it’s going to be all the more crucial that you disinfect between uses (ideally before and after each trim). “Make sure you have tapped out the hair trapped inside to avoid clogging,” adds Simone. “For a disinfectant, I would use a sterilizing alcohol pad or barber’s disinfectant, and just wipe the tool gently dry.”.

Simone (who is professionally mononymous) is a celebrity men’s groomer. Her A-List clients include Mahershala Ali, Ramy Youssef, Jason Schwartzman, John Magaro, and Brandon Perea.

Adam Hurly has been covering men's grooming for GQ since 2016. He also writes about travel. Adam is a Sioux Falls, SD native, University of Kansas graduate, former New Yorker, and current expat in Berlin. His favorite season is Oscar Season, his favorite book is Dinner At the Homesick Restaurant, and he is a proud superfan of Survivor.

Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that if you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Industry observers note that whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Recent findings suggest that toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

In a recent development, add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Sources indicate that add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (871 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor.
  • Let’s be clear: there are no age-specific makeup rules.
  • It has been revealed that before choosing colors, take a look at your current products to assess textures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Let’s be clear: there are no age-specific makeup rules. Wear whatever shade or trend you feel best in, no matter your age. That mentioned, it’s no secret that our facial features change as we get older, and to keep looking your best, the skin care and makeup products in your rotation may need to be adjusted accordingly. After 40, that powder eye shadow that once looked perfect across a smooth eyelid may now crease and settle into fine lines. Or your signature eyeliner may have started to look a little less visible because of eyelid hooding. Maybe your lashes are more sparse? Before dumping your entire eye makeup kit, take some cues from a pro on choosing and wearing the best eye makeup after 40.

It has been revealed that before choosing colors, take a look at your current products to assess textures. “As we get older, the skin on our eyelids gets thinner, and a little more crinkled, so heavy or dry powder shadows can settle into fine lines and actually emphasize them,” celebrity makeup artist Brandy Allen tells ELLE. You’ll want to swap out chalky, dry formats for cream-based shadows and liners.

In a recent development, how you treat the skin in your eye area matters too—both for how well and how long the makeup wears. Allen recommends using an eye cream or eye patches to hydrate the skin. “I have been loving the Parivie Smooth & Brighten Eye Masks because of the collagen and skin-loving ingredients they have,” indicates Allen. “Give the leftover serum a minute to sink in, and then go in with a thin layer of primer like the Urban Decay Eyeshadow Primer Potion so your shadow has something to grip onto and stays crease-free all day,” Allen suggests.

It has been revealed that many hybrid products now combine skin care with color cosmetics. A win-win for aging skin. Look for hydrating ingredients like hyaluronic acid, smoothing niacinamide, ceramides, and squalene that will treat skin while delivering solid color payoff.

Saie SuperSuede Baked Eyeshadow.

16-hour wear; infused with jojoba esters, ceramides, hyaluronic acid, squalane.

Laura Mercier Matte Caviar Stick Eye Shadow.

Available in 32 shades; waterproof and sweatproof; formulated with hyaluronic acid and firming raspberry stem cell extract.

RMS Beauty Eyelights Cream Eyeshadow.

Comes in 11 colors; buildable; has antioxidant-rich green tea extract and a smoothing natural peptide quinoa extract.

ILIA The Necessary Eyeshadow Palette.

A mix of matte, satin, and metallic finishes; formulated with moisturizing jojoba seed oil and antioxidant-rich vitamin E.

It has been revealed that look for creamy formulas that blend easily like the M.A.C Dazzleshadow Eye Shadow Stick. These will crease less. “It has a soft metallic shine and 12-hour wear, and it doubles as a liner, so it’s an easy one-step product,” Allen notes.

According to recent reports, satin and soft-sheen finishes are the best here, too. Allen indicates they give the lid a little luminosity that reflects light, which makes the eye area look more lifted and fresh. “A finely milled shimmer on the center of the lid is great too, especially for the holidays. If you prefer a powder, I love the Jones Road The Best Eyeshadow. It has a soft texture that blends out so easily, and it comes in both matte and shimmer finishes.”.

Allen says soft, warm neutrals like taupes, espresso and chocolate browns, bronze, and soft rose gold tones are most flattering for 40 and over eyes. “I’d also recommend swapping a jet-black liner for a deep brown. Brown still defines the eye but looks softer and less harsh against the skin.” Allen’s top pick is the Glampton Cream Eyeshadow & Gel Liner Duo in Espresso & Rose Gold, which she says is a great option here because it gives you both shades in one. “The shadow stick is creaseless, blends out with just your finger, and the gel liner glides on without tugging on the lid,” Allen notes.

In a recent development, just because your skin is maturing doesn’t mean you can’t try trends. Allen says it’s more about adjusting the trend to work for you. “The lived-in, smudged smoky eye trend is actually great for more mature skin; just keep it soft, and focus the liner on the outer half of the lower lash line instead of going all the way around,” says Allen. One product she suggests avoiding is chunky glitter, as it can settle into lines and emphasize texture.

It has been revealed that once your products are in place, perfect your application technique. It’ll make a difference. “When blending shadow, angle it upward toward the tail of your brow instead of dragging it down. This gives the eye an instant lift,” Allen instructs. You can also tap a little rose gold or champagne shimmer onto the inner corners and center of the lid to brighten. And don’t forget the under-eyes and brows. “A color corrector like the Bobbi Brown Skin Long-Wearing Color Corrector Stick cancels out darkness, and well-groomed, filled-in brows frame the whole eye area,” Allen explains.

Industry observers note that A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless Fresh York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; rapidly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.).

In a recent development, uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A handful of things are non-negotiable at Thanksgiving. You need turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, and, of course, a slice of pie to round out your meal. And pumpkin pie is the undeniable star of the dessert table.

Sources indicate that but sometimes you're strapped for time and have too much on your plate (pun intended) to whip something up from scratch. So we tried six different grocery store pumpkin pies to find the best store-bought shortcut. And our team's verdict was pretty unanimous, even if it’s a bit hard to hear: No premade pie will ever taste as good as a homemade one.

Recent findings suggest that it primarily comes down to the crust. Frozen and pre-baked pies typically rely on vegetable-based fat instead of butter because they’re more affordable, reliable, and shelf-stable—but that comes at a cost. You not only miss out on the decadent, buttery taste, but the crusts can also leave an unpleasant film on your tongue.

That remarked, when you need to outsource to the grocery store, we found two options that will work in a pinch.

The pie that we’d feel most confident bringing to Thanksgiving dinner comes straight from the Whole Foods bakery department. That’s not to say it’s perfect, though. The crust is almost upsettingly pale, but it’s made with real butter and only a little bit of palm oil. And since it doesn’t leave a noticeable film and still lets the butter flavor shine, we’ll let this one slide.

Once you look past the crust’s color, this pie is solid overall. The filling is decadent, not too sweet, and creamy without being mushy. Whole Foods doesn’t shy away from the spices, either.

Senior Editor Samantha MacAvoy noted that the warming spices are nicely balanced, while Designer Alison Dominguez said, “The flavor was exactly how a pumpkin pie should taste.”.

Costco’s pumpkin pie isn’t perfect: The crust uses palm oil-based shortening rather than butter and can develop a soggy bottom if you buy it too far in advance. (And it doesn’t hold a candle to the warehouse’s holy grail pumpkin cheesecake.) But it has a cult following for a reason, and not just because of its $5.99 price tag.

Even with its faults, the crust has great flavor and enough salt to create a balanced bite. Dominguez appreciated how it was “flaky and not too thick, and most importantly, it let the pie filling itself shine.” News and Features Editor Amanda Mactas chose Costco’s pie as her number one pick. “It all seemed to melt together in one creamy bite,” she said.

And at over three pounds, this dessert is the indisputable champion if you want to feed a crowd for less.

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Recent findings suggest that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

According to recent reports, reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

It has been revealed that add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

Are clothing deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?
