Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (640 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately.
  • Recent findings suggest that A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce.
  • Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

Recent findings suggest that A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Sources indicate that using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

It seems that Queen Letizia of Spain is also well versed in the art of the midday shoe swap, albeit with a slightly more sophisticated, regal approach.

In a recent development, on Wednesday, the Spanish monarch joined King Felipe VI and the Austrian president and first lady, Alexander Van der Bellen and Doris Schmidauer, to inaugurate the Mariana of Austria exhibition at Madrid’s Museo Nacional del Prado, before hosting a luncheon at Zarzuela Palace. Rather than changing outfits between engagements, Letizia switched out her shoes to produce quite a different effect.

The queen opted for a burgundy pantsuit from Spanish label Bleis, comprising a single-breasted blazer and straight-leg pants, worn over a pink tie-neck blouse. She brought out the pink further by layering on a punchy, fuchsia Carolina Herrera felt coat that has been a firm favorite in her wardrobe for years.

She accessorized with a burgundy JW Pei Noor top-handle bag, pointed-toe Magrit kitten heels in a matching shade of leather, and zigzagging diamond earrings by Bárbara Goenaga, neatly rounding out her royal ensemble.

Come lunchtime, Letizia had traded her pointed pumps for a pair of pale pink patent Sézane Paula Babies: a rounded toe, double strap, and sturdy block heel shoe. The French label’s retro-inflected Mary Janes have become something of a wardrobe staple for the royal, who owns them in no fewer than five colorways. Her morning’s footwear emphasized the sharpness of her tailoring, while the second pair brought a sweeter sensibility to suiting.

Recent findings suggest that burgundy and pink proved itself a popular color combo on the fall 2026 runways, particularly at Chanel under Matthieu Blazy, with wider shades of red and pink at Celine. Queen Letizia has long had a knack for making the season’s more adventurous color trends work within the parameters of her royal wardrobe, too. Earlier this month, on a visit to Campus Diversia, she teamed a pair of navy corduroy pants with chocolate-brown outerwear and sturdy boots. Over the summer, she embraced yellow in a gathered Adolfo Domínguez dress flecked with other pastel shades. And who could forget her coronation weekend wardrobe all the way back 2023, when she went from a zesty green Victoria Beckham dress to a head-to-toe Barbie pink ensemble?

What compounds the Spanish royal’s elegant sense of style is that so much of it is defined by pieces she’s had for years, reconfigured according to her schedule or the prevailing fashion mood. With a swift change of shoes or a refreshed color combo, you needn’t have the resources of a royal wardrobe to pull it off.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

According to recent reports, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

According to recent reports, uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

It has been revealed that it was a lifesaver for me when I was single (before I could sweetly ask my partner to do the job)—and so simple that shaving my back almost became fun. I would use it directly in the shower, making for easy cleanup. (Though never with the shower running; it's waterproof, but I didn't want the handle getting slippery enough that I’d drop it.) I never had any issues with nicking or razor burn with the Intellimax Pro’s main trimming head, though it was trickier to get a uniform shave using the foil shaving head. Frankly, it was easier to just use the .5mm trimming head every day if I wanted to stay stubble-free. Adam Hurly.

According to recent reports, the Slimmer’s compact head is its main attraction. There’s less machine to maneuver around tight spots, with two combs for leaving some length and a light for a better view – it stays off when you first switch the device on, and another press of the power button brings it into play. USB-C charging also saves you packing another cable. I just wish Meridian had included a pouch – with a trimmer this small and two loose combs, it feels like an obvious omission.

Sources indicate that its two combs cover 1.6mm or 4mm of hair length, so there’s some choice when you don’t want to take everything off. If you prefer longer chest hair, the longer guards on Meridian's Original model make more sense. Still, the Slimmer is the device I’d pick when close control over a blade matters most.

Long-term testing notes: I relied on the Slimmer for around a month on my chest and below the belt. The narrow head made awkward spots easier to navigate, and it cut through thick hair without pulling or nicking me. Without a comb, it left a hint of stubble I was happy with, although the Philips 5000’s foil gets smoother results. As for its ergonomics? The soft, grippy handle was comfortable, and the hinged blade made it easy to rinse out trapped hair. Esat Dedezade.

Recent findings suggest that the OneBlade arrived on the scene years back as a hybrid between an electric trimmer/shaver and a manual razor, with replaceable cartridges ensuring you always had the sharpest cutting surface. The Intimate SkinProtect version steps up the game with coated teeth that protect against bites without compromising on stubble maintenance. For truly sensitive areas, I’d still recommend using the low-profile buffer guard to prevent friction or snips. And if you’re already a OneBlade owner, you can just buy the Intimate SkinProtect cartridges, and swap them on when you start working below the neck.

Recent findings suggest that right out of the box, the Black Ops inspires confidence with its well-weighted, stainless-steel build—wrapped in a grippy rubber handle to eliminate any chance of a slip. While it may sound like something you’d download for your PS5, the Manscaper Black Ops isn’t playing any games when it comes to getting the job done. The trimmer arrives with eight guards ranging from 1.5–13 millimeters, as well as an adjustable guide comb to give you more options for your hair down there. And, like its amphibious namesake, the Manscaper Black Ops is fully waterproof.

Industry observers note that we look for trimmers that can get through thick growth without pulling and are easy to control when we get to the awkward bits. We pay attention to how securely the guards fit, how comfortably the handle turns around the body, and how much work it takes to get a smooth finish. Cleaning, battery life, and charging matter, too, especially with a tool that may cover several grooming jobs.

Recent findings suggest that adam Hurly and Dean Stattmann bring their grooming reviews and health and wellness coverage to this guide, For this update, Esat Dedezade has also drawn on his body-groomer testing for British GQ. The entries identify whose findings support each recommendation, and advice from celebrity groomer Dan Perri helps explain what to look for and how to maintain the tools.

What to Look For in a Body Hair Trimmer.

In a recent development, for a professional opinion on what to prioritize when buying an electric shaver or grooming kit, we sought out the expertise of celebrity groomer Dan Perri, who keeps A-list clients like Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser looking tidy. Here are the key attributes of a good body hair trimmer, says Perri:.

How do you maintain a body hair trimmer?

According to recent reports, “If you want the best performance out of your trimmer, keeping the blade clean and lubricated is key,” indicates Perri. “Oiling the trimmer every few weeks will keep the blade running smooth, prevent any pulling of the hair, and keep the blade temperature down.” He adds that most trimmers come with a small supply of mineral oil—use it. (Wahl sells a great 4-oz clipper oil for cheap, too.) Be sure to use a machine-safe disinfectant spray to help keep the blade sanitized, which will prevent breakouts, Perri adds.

Can you use a beard trimmer for manscaping?

Sources indicate that some beard trimmers are designed for use on the body, but only if they have attachments designed to keep skin from being pulled into the blade. Keep in mind that the ergonomics of a great beard trimmer doesn’t necessarily align with the ergonomics you’ll want for shaving body parts. You’ll have a harder time hitting hard to reach places, like the back. And beyond that, you’ll want to aggressively sanitize any trimming heads and guards that touch both your face and your… [looks down].

What is the best body hair trimmer for men?

In a recent development, we recommend the Philips Norelco All-in-One 7000 Series for most people who want to keep some length on their body hair. The 3mm and 5mm body combs let you choose how much to leave. For a smooth finish, go with the Body Groomer 5000 Series and its dedicated foil head.

How often should I trim my body hair?

In a recent development, depends! If you want to be as smooth as an Olympic swimmer, you might want to shave every day. If that's too much of a hassle, doing it every two or three days can be sufficient to have you smooth without your stubble scratching up your shirts.

Should I shave off all of my body hair?

Do you find body hair unsightly? Then maybe you want to shave your body hair to give yourself a smoother appearance. The decision to trim body hair usually depends on what you or even your partner prefers. For professional sports, a hairless body might be preferred for an advantage, like for swimmers or wrestlers.

Is it better to trim body hair when it's wet or dry?

You can shave your hair whether it's wet or dry, but we prefer doing it on dry hair. Trimmers are able to more easily cut through the hair when it's dry, and you can get more even cuts if you're not going for a clean shave. (Though wet/dry trimmers are all over the market.).

What are common manscaping mistakes?

Besides using non-skinsafe grooming electricals (we got you covered in that department), some common manscaping mishaps are the result of poor technique (shaving against the grain), not trimming on cleansed, exfoliated skin, and neglecting post-shaving moisturizing—especially if you have sensitive skin.

Sources indicate that razor burn is no joke. Preparing the skin, using proper shaving technique, and including lotions, moisturizers, and other skin car products into you grooming routine are all good ways to prevent razor burn.

Dan Perri is a celebrity groomer based between NYC, LA, and Florida. His A-list clients include Post Malone, Gerard Butler, and Brendan Fraser.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.
  • The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.
  • Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, mentioned Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

It has been revealed that “I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”.

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

In a recent development, it’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for fresh members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

In a recent development, “I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build major things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of newly introduced well-paying union jobs.”.

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., remarked in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

In a recent development, there’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the latest Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

Industry observers note that “One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., stated in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”.

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

In a recent development, absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

According to recent reports, “The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

In a recent development, “All I know is you better not burn no turkey. That’s a culinary crime,” the Grammy-winning singer told Delish. And if you're cooking without a backup bird? You might want to pay especially close attention to that oven. “You better get it right on the first try.”.

She's no longer making pig feet these days, but the other familiar favorites have stuck around. Ciara says those dishes still “make me very happy,” which is as good a reason as any to keep a family tradition going.

Personally, I think we’ve been limiting Thanksgiving dinner to one holiday for far too long.

According to recent reports, after forming a fast friendship on Celebrity Substantial Brother U.K., JoJo Siwa and Chris Hughes sparked public interest with their growing bond. In the weeks following the show, the pair traveled together, spent time with each other’s families, and shared increasingly affectionate posts online, further fueling speculation about a possible romance. Now, the couple has reportedly called it quits. Here’s everything we know about their relationship.

Siwa and Hughes were both contestants on Celebrity Substantial Brother U.K.. At the time, Siwa was still in a relationship with Australian actor Kath Ebbs. However, viewers took note of her chemistry with Hughes, especially during emotional moments in the house.

“We’re very similar in our energy, in our outlook on life,” Siwa added. “Chris was there for me at my lowest times and I was there for him at his lowest times. That’s what made it so special.”.

In a recent development, she also praised Hughes’s reaction to the homophobic comments she received on the show, saying, “That highlighted Chris’s true personality and it was beautiful to see. People obviously say what they want about people, but that showed me who he really is.”.

Speculation about Siwa and Hughes’s relationship continued, especially after the two traveled together and began appearing in each other’s social media posts.

On July 12, Hughes told The Sun’s Fabulous Magazine about his relationship with Siwa.

Industry observers note that “Our first kiss was genuinely special—it felt like I was in a movie,” he explained. “I can’t keep my hands off her now.”.

Siwa continued to speak candidly about her relationship with Hughes while attending the Hannah Montana 20th anniversary special premiere in Los Angeles.

“The inspiration behind that is my very sweet love Christopher,” she told People of her upcoming single “Serendipity.”.

“Well, our lives connecting and meeting are like serendipity. It’s my favorite word, so I had to write a song about it.”.

Hughes commented on the post, “absolute cinemmmmmma 👏🏼.”.

According to recent reports, siwa and Hughes discovered they share the exact same vision for her dream engagement ring. #157830. The Rise, Fall, and Future of Makeup Artist-Led Brands

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Vogue ↗ Open Full Page

The Rise, Fall, and Future of Makeup Artist-Led Brands

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2305 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When news broke in October that Isamaya Ffrench had severed ties with her namesake beauty brand, fans of the avant-garde makeup artist were saddened but not surprised.
  • Ffrench responded to a customer complaint on Instagram in October by apologizing, adding that she was no longer associated with the brand.
  • According to recent reports, though Isamaya Beauty remains operational, speculation about its future has been rife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When news broke in October that Isamaya Ffrench had severed ties with her namesake beauty brand, fans of the avant-garde makeup artist were saddened but not surprised. For months, there had been growing customer frustration about unfulfilled orders and unresponsive support. Buyers reported severe shipping delays, missing or damaged items, and unanswered refund requests across the brand’s Instagram and review sites like Trustpilot. By July, its social media accounts had stopped creating new posts, while inventory markdowns on its website were as high as 70%.

Ffrench responded to a customer complaint on Instagram in October by apologizing, adding that she was no longer associated with the brand. Shortly after, she thanked her followers on her personal Instagram during what she called “an incredibly difficult and emotional time”. The Isamaya Beauty brand did not respond to a request for comment.

According to recent reports, though Isamaya Beauty remains operational, speculation about its future has been rife. It follows the bankruptcy of fellow makeup artist Pat McGrath’s eponymous label earlier in January. Pat McGrath Labs famously hit a $1 billion valuation in 2018, a mere three years after launch, but struggled to scale and keep pace with modern beauty demands. It exited the Chapter 11 bankruptcy process in April under newly introduced majority owner GDA Luma, a Miami-based investment firm. McGrath herself stepped down as CEO and transferred her equity to the holding tech giant while staying on as chief creative officer.

While Ffrench and McGrath remain highly respected creative forces (McGrath is the creative director of cosmetics for La Beauté Louis Vuitton, while Ffrench presently runs the interdisciplinary concept store and gallery Studio Iron), the hurdles faced by their namesake labels highlight the structural friction between avant-garde artistry and commercial scaling. Their trajectories also signal a broader reckoning for makeup artist (MUA) brands, which have become a dominant yet deeply volatile segment of the beauty market, characterized by rapid boom-and-bust cycles.

Recent findings suggest that the late 2010s marked an unprecedented period of rapid industry growth. Social media, viral debuts, and Sephora shelf space helped drive hype for makeup artist-led brands, several of which subsequently enjoyed massive funding and bloated valuations. Many, however, struggled with post-pandemic relevance and debt. Today, the market has become saturated, and shoppers are increasingly fatigued by frequent drops and buzzwords. Consumer preferences are also evolving, with Gen Z opting for customizable, skin-first routines while millennials desire substantive education beyond surface-level trends.

According to recent reports, “On the back of the success of brands like Charlotte Tilbury, which grew and ultimately sold to a strategic buyer, more people became interested in putting in capital behind the next generation [of MUAs],” indicates Ilya Seglin, managing director of consumer, retail and e-commerce at Cascadia Capital, citing Patrick Ta, Makeup by Mario, Danessa Myricks Beauty and Westman Atelier. However, many of these brands have not been acquired. Their founders have spoken publicly about choosing to stay independent and fund long-term growth, but at the same time, beauty strategic investors have pulled back on makeup deals.

Charlotte Tilbury at the opening of her Covent Garden, London flagship in 2025.

According to recent reports, as Seglin explains, “Strategics have no idea how to get comfortable with color [cosmetics]”, which is increasingly viewed by investors as a “fashion” category — in other words, a volatile, trend-driven sector that is high risk but high reward. Both fashion and MUA-founded labels share the challenges of maintaining quarterly growth while mitigating trend fatigue and inventory risk. Beauty trend cycles, in particular, have accelerated with the advent of online algorithms and short-form content that create rapid microtrends that can rise, peak, and fade within weeks or months, rather than years. “The perceived risk profile of color brands has increased, so strategics have become more cautious. They don’t know if this is like a fashion brand that’s going to be around for 5-10 years, or whether it’s going to be around for longer. Strategics want to acquire brands that are going to be around forever.”.

It has been revealed that despite the risks, makeup artist brands remain attractive to customers, accounting for roughly 30% of the prestige beauty market in the US, according to Larissa Jensen, senior vice president and global beauty industry advisor at Circana. “Makeup artist brands are the largest brand type within the makeup category. Collectively, they’re growing about 7%, which is outpacing total makeup growth,” she explains. “The units are actually performing, up 5%, compared to makeup overall, which was flat. That’s an indicator of demand.”.

Industry observers note that still, MUAs have come a long way since early pioneers Bobbi Brown (1991), François Nars (1994) and Laura Mercier (1996) disrupted traditional department-store beauty, bringing their backstage and editorial expertise to everyday consumers via wearable neutrals and face base products. The subsequent rise of Instagram and YouTube transformed makeup artists like Charlotte Tilbury into global personalities. By the late 2010s, A-list celebrities and influencers (think Kylie Cosmetics by Kylie Jenner, Fenty Beauty by Rihanna and Rare Beauty by Selena Gomez) flooded the market. Meanwhile, contract manufacturing enabled independent, founder-led brands (like Glossier and Morphe) and beauty vloggers with massive, highly trusting audiences (such as Huda Kattan and Jaclyn Hill) to launch swiftly and market directly to consumers. Built-in audiences and excited VCs temporarily overshadowed traditional artist-founded lines.

Bobbi Brown applying makeup on model backstage at Tory Burch SS07.

Recent findings suggest that as consumers grow weary of celebrity white-label lines, credibility is shifting back to working makeup artists. Mary Phillips (M.ph Beauty) and Mario Dedivanovic (Makeup by Mario), for instance, regularly share behind-the-scenes details, signature techniques and product breakdowns from their red carpet prep with the likes of the Kardashian-Jenners. Both artists have long been part of the family’s glam squad and turned their routines into global beauty trends and brands.

Meanwhile, some modern founders didn’t come from traditional channels like celebrity glam or print magazines, but can demonstrate why their formulas deserve permanent space in one’s bag. Jamie Genevieve, for example, built an online following after working on makeup counters in Scotland. Her beauty brand Vieve celebrates its sixth anniversary this month. Sales have grown from £6.5 million in 2024 to £9.3 million by late 2026. Meanwhile, Jordana Ticia’s eponymous label has become one of the UK’s biggest indie beauty success stories in recent years, marked by a 239% increase in TikTok Shop GMV in 2024 (two years after joining the platform) and a May 2026 launch into Space NK where first-week sales beat forecasts, according to the Manchester-based founder.

Recent findings suggest that many of these modern MUA brands are actively pushing back against traditional “haul” culture by highlighting durability, multi-season versatility and cost-per-wear. Rather than lean heavily on novelty collaborations or viral packaging, the new generation is more focused on approachable, everyday beauty staples that can become high-repeat categories.

Industry observers note that violette, founded in 2021 by the Parisian makeup artist Violette Serrat, has leaned into French attitudes to beauty: to age with ease and feel comfortable in one’s own skin, and to treat skincare and fragrance like food or wine — something to savor and enjoy. Instead of seeking to mask or fix perceived flaws, Serrat — who has amassed over a million followers collectively across her personal Instagram and YouTube accounts — encourages natural-looking, lived-in looks. Her routines often show her applying products with her fingers rather than complex tools.

Violette is inspired by makeup artist Violette Serrat's love for fine art and French beauty philosophy.

Violette’s go-to market strategy was not to launch in Sephora or an equivalent retailer. Instead, the brand debuted in locations like Oh My Cream, a “clean beauty” concept store, and French pharmacies, which in her view offered a real “stamp of approval” given their penchant for products that are simple, consistent and credible. Violette’s top sellers include the Bisou Balm (a lipstick-balm hybrid that creates a soft, blurred look) and Boum Boum Milk (a 3-in-1 skincare spray combining toner, serum and moisturizer).

Sources indicate that serrat’s belief is that while brands don’t have to speak to everyone, their products need to be universally understood. “I think it’s ok to be a little bit more niche. But my mission as a makeup artist is to simplify my technique,” explains Serrat, whose makeup has appeared editorially in American and French Vogue, and on the red carpet via figures such as Léa Seydoux and Natalia Vodianova. “If you look at my work, it’s very complex makeup. But for my brand, I want to make sure my products are understood on an instinctual level. You just put your finger in and do it.”.

Industry observers note that the British makeup artist Katie Jane Hughes, who counts a total of over two million followers across TikTok and Instagram, also bridges playful artistry with accessible, skin-first education. Rather than pushing rigid beauty rules or complicated tutorials, Hughes offers practical breakdowns and techniques that let natural skin texture show through. After years of working with high-profile clients such as Emmy Rossum, Kerry Washington, and Dua Lipa, among others, Hughes — who is based in Latest York — founded her beauty brand KJH in 2023, selling a tight lineup of accessibly priced items including the Precision Sculpture Stylo (a sculpting liner for the lips or eyes) and Microscara (a mascara with a petite brush built for better control). Sales have grown 250% year on year.

Sources indicate that core to KJH is its ability to reach a wide demographic of people. A poll conducted independently by KJH found that only 10% of the brand’s customers are makeup artists or fellow creatives. “Most of the people are not professionals. So I wanted to create products that allow them to feel like they’re more of an expert with what’s in their makeup bag,” claims Hughes. As of August, the brand has expanded from DTC into Sephora in the US and Canada. Asked whether it’s a pivot in strategy, Hughes explains that cosmetics are deeply sensory products that rely on in-person testing and trust. “I like playing with a product in person before buying it. I think that’s really notable.”.

British makeup artist Katie Jane Hughes has won over a loyal audience for her approachable tutorials, signature glowing aesthetic and rule-breaking attitude toward beauty.

Built on technical skill and real-world experience, makeup artist-founded brands continue to stand out from celebrity or creator cash-grab lines. More are also expected to come to market, with the next highly anticipated launch to potentially come from celebrity makeup artist Nina Park, if early trademark filings are any indication. However, as Circana’s Jensen warns, “how many of [those MUA labels] really blow up and become huge or mainstays remains to be seen.”.

It has been revealed that indeed, Violette, which is not yet profitable, raised $5 million from three existing investors in May, extending the Series B round that originally closed in 2024. It’s significantly smaller than the earlier sky-high multiples some MUA labels have previously commanded. Nonetheless, the recent funding indicates investor optimism and wider appetite for Violette, which Serrat is confident can reach profitability in the short term. The brand has entered latest doors, including Sephora in the US as of 2025 and the UK this November. According to Serrat, sales at Sephora have doubled year over year, and the brand has since been “fast-tracked” to roll out in 800 doors, including in Canada, up from 80.

Taking on investment means toeing the line between creativity and commerciality. “If you’re niche, you cannot have investors,” she states, matter-of-factly. “You can do a super niche and creative brand, but you have to be self-funded. For me, raising money made me anxious. I needed to make sure I was able to have a very healthy business. You can create a brand that is inspiring, but at the same time, you need to think of the bottom line. It’s my obsession. I want to be profitable as soon as I can.”.

It’s for these reasons KJH is primarily self-funded and has operated without traditional outside venture capital or institutional funding rounds since its launch. Hughes stressed the need to work at her own pace, despite ongoing interest from incubators and VCs alike. “I didn’t want to be tied to anybody. I didn’t want to feel like I had this substantial company above me telling me what I should do next,” she explains. “Now, we have more of a steady flow of sales, allowing us to have more releases throughout the year. We’ll probably release two to three products a year versus just one. But it’s because I want to do it. I want to do what’s right for me and my community.”.

Hughes's beauty brand KJH focuses on multi-use formulas and practical makeup education.

However, experts also say that more than ever, consumers are looking to credible industry leaders and specialized experts to cut through the noise and AI-driven information overload. “For makeup artists, it’s really about bringing forth their expertise. There’s an authenticity that comes with their brands,” claims Jensen. “Within the hair category, salon brands are the largest. Within skincare, it’s clinical brands founded by doctors or cosmetic chemists. What that collectively says about the consumer is that they are looking for expertise in their categories.”.

Seglin adds that investor sentiment — like consumer trends — is cyclical. And the current funding constraints may, in fact, be beneficial for both the market and MUAs. “It forces them to actually be good. They will probably be better businesses than the brands that were flooded with investor cash before.” Those eager for a payout need to “be realistic about market dynamics”, he indicates. “If your expectation is to raise $10 million to launch a brand and in three years you’re going to sell to L’Oréal, I would temper those aspirations.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a massive, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Recent findings suggest that bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.).

In a recent development, broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Industry observers note that remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The following article contains minor spoilers for The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

It might seem strange, the notion that people have been surprised to find that a David Fincher film, written by Quentin Tarantino and starring Brad Pitt, is “actually good.” But moviegoers had their fair share of reasons to be skeptical of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth: chief among them, that Tarantino was forcing a mind-melding of the auteurs that could prove disastrously incongruous simply because he didn’t want to blow his long-awaited 10th and final film on a sequel. The 10-film rule is, of course, completely self-imposed, a mandate Tarantino is stubbornly sticking to instead of realizing he can still employ strict curation and quality control without limiting his filmography to a perfect even number. But now that he’s actually, finally, on what will be his last movie (according to his rules), there’s this notion that he’s afraid to pull the trigger—which some believe he all but confirmed when, in 2023, he announced his 10th film would be called The Movie Critic, only to completely retract that a month later.

Two years later, Tarantino sat down as a guest on (what else?) The Church of Tarantino podcast, hosted by two QT superfans, which is actually a pretty fun listen in between all the excessive stanning. So rapidly do they bring up QT10 that it’s obvious the director was anxious to set the record straight. Tarantino tells the hosts that TMC started as an exercise in attempting to write a compelling story about “the most boring” profession imaginable. Despite succeeding, he realized he wasn’t excited by it once the film entered pre-production. There was also a version of the story that he adapted into an eight-hour miniseries, until he realized he had no interest in the process of selling and making TV either.

It has been revealed that it’s similar to the way he’s talked about what became Cliff Booth, which started as a novel before morphing into an unwieldy feature script until Pitt convinced him to let someone else take a crack at directing it, lest these titular misadventures go to waste. Watching the film last week, my ears perked up when, in the midst of being courted by Cliff, high-powered Hollywood agent Karen Crosby reveals she got her start in the industry as a… movie critic. She reflects back on her time writing about film derisively, describing the profession as one with a low barrier for entry.

Recent findings suggest that karen is instantly one of the most beguiling characters in a movie filled with colorful performances both major and small. Played by Elizabeth Debicki with an icy, over-it resolve, Karen’s nagging fascination with Cliff makes for what one critic aptly described as Tarantino’s best-written romance since Jackie Brown. Despite being the closest thing to a co-lead, you walk away from the film feeling like you haven’t seen nearly enough of her.

Later in the film, Debicki gets a showy, highlight reel-worthy monologue where Karen, instead of extolling the virtues of cinema as a former critic might, recites what’s apparently an infamous credo among her close friends: that film, while entertaining, hardly rises to the level of being true art. (This is much to the delight of one of her clients, A-list TV star Charlie Peters, played by Scott Caan.).

Industry observers note that it was at this point that I was certain we were watching remixed and repurposed scenes from The Movie Critic—and that if Karen Crosby wasn’t the eponymous character, she was at the very least a gender-flipped version. In one of the only times Tarantino talked openly about his erstwhile film, he noted it would be “based on a guy who really lived but was never really famous, and he used to write movie reviews for a porno rag.” Meanwhile, the internet ran with the idea that the film would actually be a not-so-thinly-veiled tribute to Pauline Kael. Karen, for what it’s worth, name-drops Kael when describing her past life.

That this is among the best scenes in the otherwise thoroughly enjoyable Further Mis-Adventures only underscores how silly Tarantino’s 10-film imposition is. Look, l I agree with him: as a logline, it hardly sounds exciting enough to be a career finale, but a Tarantino-directed version of the movie probably would’ve been a good time given how much the director clearly enjoys luxuriating in this world. He can write odes to ‘60s and ‘70s cinema in his sleep. But because it would be a retread with no 11th script to follow, it’ll never see the light of day.

Or will it? I hate to enable weird science, but The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth doesn’t simply work; it’s one of the best movies of the year. Can another director submit himself to Tarantino’s tone and vision the way Fincher does so gamely here? Would Fincher even want to do that again? Hard to say on both fronts, but if Tarantino is going to keep being precious about his next (last?) directorial outing, the least he could do is let someone else execute his other ideas before they start collecting dust. Even Tarantino’s B-Tier is still a great time at the movies.

Sources indicate that delish editors handpick every product we feature. We may earn commission from the links on this page.

Whether it was roasting a chicken, pouring an outrageously large Cosmopolitan, or just organizing her pantry, I’d happily watch Ina Garten do just about anything on television. But there’s apparently one TV gig that even the Barefoot Contessa can't stomach, and I’m a little devastated we’ll never get to see it.

During the November 18 episode of her Happy Hour with Ina Garten podcast, Garten got to talking with guest Rose Byrne about opportunities that felt too intimidating to pursue. Ina didn’t have to think very hard to come up with her own example.

It has been revealed that “Somebody asked me to do Dancing with the Stars,” she revealed. “I thought, ‘Nobody needs to see that. That’s not happening.’”.

With which I respectfully disagree. I think quite a few of us would happily clear our schedules to see Ina Garten attempt a salsa. Unfortunately, Garten wasn’t particularly eager to find out how she'd fare in the ballroom. “The closer I got to the day when I had to do it, the more I’d have nightmares,” she admitted.

Byrne was sympathetic, acknowledging that she’d be terrified of competing, too.

Sources indicate that still, this is a woman who’s made some pretty bold decisions throughout her career. Garten left her job working on nuclear energy policy in Washington, D.C., to buy a specialty food store in the Hamptons with virtually no experience running one. There were some early mishaps, including a batch of roast chickens nobody wanted until she changed how they were displayed, and those experiences eventually helped shape the approachable cooking philosophy behind her hugely successful cookbooks.

And Garten has certainly gotten comfortable sharing the spotlight over the years. In Delish’s recent interview with Garten and Jennifer Garner, the longtime friends traded stories about their kitchen adventures, favorite recipes, and even late-night In-N-Out Burger runs. Give Ina some good food and someone she loves spending time with, and she's in her element.

Personally, though, I can't stop imagining Jeffrey in the audience holding up a giant “10” sign in support of his wife. We really missed out on something special.
